title: NAHB special study: Government Regulation in the Price of a New Home: 2026

history.reason: Source read directly on the access date; findings transcribed from the document.

publisher: National Association of Home Builders (Economics and Housing Policy)
reliability: Published by the national home builders trade association, which advocates for lower regulation; survey of its own members with small samples and self-reported costs.
findings: NAHB surveyed a panel of 2,125 NAHB members with land development experience in March 2026; 54 developers gave complete and useable responses. Builder questions were special questions in the March 2026 NAHB/Wells Fargo HMI; 337 builders gave complete and useable responses.

NAHB estimates regulation accounts for $131,734 of the $499,500 average new-home price (26.4%): $46,975 during development and $84,939 during construction (the table shows $46,795 for development; the document is internally inconsistent by $180).

Of builders surveyed, 93.4% reported that regulation caused some delay in the construction process; where delay existed it averaged a little over six weeks. NAHB computes the "pure" cost of construction-phase delay at $1,632 per home (0.3% of house price).
Of developers, 94.2% said complying with regulations typically caused a delay, averaging roughly seven months; pure cost of development-phase delay $2,480 per home (0.5%).

Builder-paid fees after buying the lot (which can include building permit or inspection fees) average 4.0% of final house price ($20,154); changes to building codes over the past 10 years 8.1% ($40,288).

The builder question on delay asks how much extra time complying with regulations "(including unreasonable delays in obtaining permits or inspections)" adds to construction; permit delay is not separated from inspection delay or other regulation.
NAHB Appendix A assumes 1.3 months from lot sale to start of construction, taken from Census Survey of Construction data for homes built for sale in 2020.
limitations: Survey respondents are NAHB members; response rate for developers is 54 of 2,125 panel members; builders were drawn from the HMI panel, which is stratified by builder size but whose size breakdown of respondents was not read.
Costs and delays are self-reported by members of an advocacy group; not independently measured.
Permit approval time (application to issuance) is not reported separately, and remodelers are not covered (single-family new construction only).
Dollar totals not recomputed except noting the $46,975 vs $46,795 inconsistency.
